extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: MPEP guidance for determining whether a claim 'recites' an abstract idea under Step 2A Prong One of the Alice/Mayo framework, including enumerated groupings of abstract ideas, examples of non-abstract claims, and procedural directions for examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' Step 2A Prong One procedure for identifying abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation(s) fall within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and is eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B), unless the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon). See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3) for rare exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office distills relevant case law into three enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent and are intended to shift examiners from a case-by-case comparison approach to generally applying the body of case law across technologies and claim types. Groupings are not mutually exclusive; a claim limitation may fall within more than one grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law identifies many concepts as falling within this grouping (e.g., methods for converting binary-coded decimal to pure binary (Benson); formulas for alarm limits (Flook); Arrhenius equation (Diehr); mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski)). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim actually recites the mathematical concept or merely is based on or involves one. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into this grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols; words operating on data can serve the same purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or symbols (e.g., pressure = F/A, relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of relationships recited in claims include Arrhenius-style relationships, conversions between number systems, geometrical relations (antenna conductor lengths/angles), and organization/manipulation of information through mathematical correlations (Digitech). If the relationship itself is recited, that supports treating the limitation as a mathematical concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a numerical formula or equation (or textual equivalents like 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating F = ma') are within the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: specific electromagnetic standing wave formulas, Arrhenius equation, alarm-limit formulas, hedging formulas. Textual descriptions that are effectively a formula should be considered as reciting a mathematical equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical calculation is a mathematical operation or act of calculating using mathematical methods (e.g., arithmetic operations, exponentiation, statistical analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting operations such as performing resampled statistical analysis, computing alarm-limit values, converting coordinates using formulae, performing calculations to manage insurance policies, or other algorithmic computations should be considered as reciting mathematical calculations when the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification encompasses such calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping covers concepts relating to (a) fundamental economic principles or practices, (b) commercial or legal interactions, and (c) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'certain' limits the grouping to the enumerated sub-groupings; it is not to be expanded beyond them except in rare circumstances (§ 2106.04(a)(3)). The number of people involved is not dispositive; determine whether the activity falls within one of the sub-groupings. Activity of a person interacting with a computer may fall within this grouping if the activity itself matches a sub-grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes economic concepts such as hedging, insurance, mitigating risk, and other concepts relating to the economy and commerce that courts have identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Fundamental’ does not mean the practice must be old; novel price-optimization methods or new wagering rules have been classified as fundamental economic practices. Case examples: Bilski (hedging), Bancorp (insurance), Alice (intermediated settlement). The presence of familiar calculations or conventional activity used to implement the economic concept supports treating it as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting contractual relationships or transaction performance guarantees (e.g., buySAFE) and other business-related interactions are examples. If the claimed interaction is essentially a commercial/legal practice, the limitation may be treated as an abstract idea under this sub-grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers concepts such as social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, and other ways of managing behavior or relationships between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sub-grouping can encompass single-person activities (e.g., a person following instructions) or multi-person activities. Determine whether the claimed activity itself fits within managing behavior/relationships; if so, classify under this sub-grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes concepts performed in the human mind, such as observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim limitation recites concepts that can be performed solely in the human mind (even if aided by conventional computer components), it may fall within the mental-processes grouping. If a limitation also fits other groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts), identify those groupings as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that do not recite an abstract idea — non-limiting examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea include: i) a printer with belt/roller/printhead/ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine with tub/drive motor/controller/housing; iii) an earring sensor for blood glucose with memory; iv) a BRCA1 sequencing method with PCR amplification and sequencing; v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory; vi) a GUI icon-rearrangement method based on usage metrics involving automatic movement; vii) a two-stage neural-network training regimen using transformed images and a second-stage negative set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate claims that, although they may be based on or involve abstract ideas at some level, do not themselves set forth an abstract idea and thus are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B). Use these as non-limiting guidance when determining whether a claim 'recites' an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may fall into multiple groupings; identify at least one (preferably all)
rubrics_metrics.description: The groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping (e.g., a calculation that could be performed mentally is both a mathematical concept and a mental process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify at least one applicable grouping, but preferably identify all groupings that apply to the limitation(s) before proceeding to Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim recites a different judicial exception, follow the corresponding analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon), examiners should follow the guidance specific to that exception (see MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude eligibility solely because the claim does not fall into the abstract-idea groupings; check for other exceptions that may render the claim ineligible and apply their respective Step 2A analyses.
